questions.question: The expression \(e^{-\ln x}\) for \(x > 0\) is equal to
questions.explanation: Given the expression for \(x > 0\): \[E = e^{-\ln x}\] Using the logarithmic power property, \(n \ln(a) = \ln(a^n)\), we can rewrite the exponent: \[-\ln x = \ln(x^{-1})\] Substituting this back into the expression: \[E = e^{\ln(x^{-1})}\] Since \(e^{\ln(f(x))} = f(x)\) for any positive function value, the expression simplifies to: \[E = x^{-1}\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) } x^{-1}}\]

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: Consider the function \(y = x^2 - 6x + 9\). The maximum value of \(y\) obtained when \(x\) varies over the interval \(2\) to \(5\) is
questions.explanation:
The given function is: \[y = f(x) = x^2 - 6x + 9 \quad \text{for } x \in [2, 5]\] To find the maximum value over the closed interval \([2, 5]\), we first find the critical points by differentiating \(y\) with respect to \(x\): \[y' = \frac{dy}{dx} = 2x - 6\] Setting \(y' = 0\) to locate the stationary points: \[2x - 6 = 0 \implies x = 3\] Since \(x = 3\) lies within our interval \([2, 5]\), we evaluate the second derivative to check its nature: \[y'' = \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 2 > 0\] Since \(y'' > 0\), the stationary point at \(x = 3\) is a point of local minimum. Therefore, the maximum value must occur at the boundaries of the interval, \(x = 2\) or \(x = 5\). Now, we evaluate the function values at the endpoints: \[\begin{aligned} \text{At } x = 2: \quad y(2) &= (2)^2 - 6(2) + 9 = 4 - 12 + 9 = 1 \\ \text{At } x = 5: \quad y(5) &= (5)^2 - 6(5) + 9 = 25 - 30 + 9 = 4 \end{aligned}\] Comparing the values, the absolute maximum value of \(y\) in the interval is: \[\max\{y(2), y(5)\} = \max\{1, 4\} = 4\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) } 4}\]
Mistakes to avoid
Do not confuse finding the stationary point (\(x=3\)) with finding the absolute maximum value. Since the parabola opens upwards (\(a > 0\)), the stationary point yields the global minimum, meaning the maximum value must be checked at the interval boundaries.

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: Given \(y = x^2 + 2x + 10\) the value of \(\left.\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=1}\) is equal to
questions.explanation: The given equation is: \[y = x^2 + 2x + 10\] To find the value of the derivative at \(x = 1\), we first differentiate \(y\) with respect to \(x\): \[\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{d}{dx}(x^2) + \frac{d}{dx}(2x) + \frac{d}{dx}(10)\] \[\frac{dy}{dx} = 2x + 2\] Now, substituting \(x = 1\) into the derivative expression: \[\left.\frac{dy}{dx}\right|_{x=1} = 2(1) + 2 = 4\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) } 4}\]

questions.question: Consider the differential equation \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1+y^2.\) Which of the following can be a particular solution of this differential equation?
questions.explanation:
Given the differential equation \[\frac{dy}{dx} = 1 + y^2\] We are required to identify a particular solution from the given options. Separating variables and Integrating, \[\int \frac{dy}{1+y^2} = \int dx\] Using \[\int \frac{dy}{1+y^2} = \tan^{-1}(y),\] we obtain \[\tan^{-1}(y) = x + C\] \[y = \tan(x+C)\] Since no initial condition is provided, \(C\) remains arbitrary. Among the given options, \[y = \tan(x+3)\] is of the required form and therefore is a valid particular solution. \[\boxed{\text{(A)}\ y = \tan(x+3)}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not write the solution as \(y=\tan(x)+C\); the constant appears inside the argument of the tangent function.

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: A complex variable \(z = x + \text{j}\,0.1\) has its real part \(x\) varying in the range \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\). Which one of the following is the locus (shown in thick lines) of \(\dfrac{1}{z}\) in the complex plane?
questions.explanation: \(z = x + j0.1\), where the real part \(x\) varies from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\), and the imaginary part is constant at \(y = 0.1\). Geometrically, this is a horizontal line in the complex \(z\)-plane. To find the locus of \(w = \frac{1}{z}\) in the complex plane: \[w = \frac{1}{x + j0.1} = \frac{x - j0.1}{(x + j0.1)(x - j0.1)} = \frac{x - j0.1}{x^2 + (0.1)^2}\] Let \(w = u + jv\), where \(u\) is the real part and \(v\) is the imaginary part: \[u = \frac{x}{x^2 + 0.01}\] \[v = \frac{-0.1}{x^2 + 0.01}\] \[x^2 + 0.01 = -\frac{0.1}{v}\] Substitute this back into the expression for \(u\) (we have to eliminate \(x\)), \[u = x \left( -\frac{v}{0.1} \right) = -10xv \implies x = -\frac{u}{10v}\] Substitute \(x\) back into the relation \(x^2 + 0.01 = -\frac{0.1}{v}\): \[\left( -\frac{u}{10v} \right)^2 + 0.01 = -\frac{0.1}{v}\] \[\frac{u^2}{100v^2} + \frac{1}{100} = -\frac{1}{10v}\] \[u^2 + v^2 = -10v\] \[u^2 + v^2 + 10v = 0\] Completing the square for \(v\): \[u^2 + (v + 5)^2 = 5^2\] This equation represents a circle in the \(w\)-plane with center: \((u, v) = (0, -5)\) and radius: \(R = 5\). \[\boxed{\text{B}}\]

questions.question: Consider a Gaussian distributed random variable with zero mean and standard deviation \(\sigma\). The value of its cumulative distribution function at the origin will be
questions.explanation:
Let \(X\) be Gaussian with mean \(0\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). The cumulative distribution function (CDF) is \[F(x)=P(X\le x)\] Since the Gaussian distribution is symmetric about its mean, \[P(X\le 0)=P(X\ge 0)=\frac{1}{2}\] Therefore, \[F(0)=P(X\le 0)=\frac{1}{2}\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) }0.5}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse the PDF value at \(x=0\) with the CDF value at \(x=0\).
  • The result is independent of the value of \(\sigma\).

questions.subject: engineering-mathematics
questions.question: It is known that two roots of the non-linear equation \(x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 = 0\) are \(1\) and \(3\). The third root will be
questions.explanation:
We are given the cubic polynomial equation: \[x^3 - 6x^2 + 11x - 6 = 0\] Let the three roots of this equation be \(\alpha\), \(\beta\), and \(\gamma\). We are given that two of the roots are: \[\alpha = 1, \quad \beta = 3\] Step 1: Apply Vieta's formulas for cubic equations
For any cubic polynomial \(x^3 + ax^2 + bx + c = 0\), the sum of the roots relates directly to the coefficient of the \(x^2\) term: \[\alpha + \beta + \gamma = -a\] Step 2: Solve for the missing third root (\(\gamma\))
From our given polynomial, \(a = -6\). Substitute the values into Vieta's root sum formula: \[1 + 3 + \gamma = -(-6)\] \[4 + \gamma = 6 \implies \gamma = 2\] The missing third root is 2, which matches Option C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 2}}\]
Key points
  • Vieta's Theorem: For a polynomial equation of degree \(n\), the sum of all roots always equals the negative of the second-leading coefficient (\(a_{n-1}\)) divided by the leading coefficient (\(a_n\)).

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: Which one of the following discrete-time systems is time-invariant?
questions.explanation:
Time invariance:
In a time invariant system, any delay provided in input must be reflected in output. (i) From option (A): \(y(n)=n\,x(n)\) Let input be delayed by \(n_0\). Then corresponding output is \[y_1(n)=n\,x(n-n_0) \tag{i}\] Now, output \(y(n)\) is delayed by \(n_0\), \[y(n-n_0)=(n-n_0)x(n-n_0) \tag{ii}\] From equations (i) and (ii), \[y_1(n)\neq y(n-n_0)\] Thus, the system is time varying. (ii) From option (B): \(y(n)=x(3n)\) Let input be delayed by \(n_0\). Then corresponding output is \[y_1(n)=x(3n-n_0) \tag{iii}\] Now, output \(y(n)\) is delayed by \(n_0\), \[y(n-n_0)=x\!\bigl[3(n-n_0)\bigr] \tag{iv}\] From equations (iii) and (iv), \[y_1(n)\neq y(n-n_0)\] Thus, the system is time varying. (iii) From option (C): \(y(n)=x(-n)\) Let input be delayed by \(n_0\). Then corresponding output is \[y_1(n)=x(-n-n_0) \tag{v}\] Now, output \(y(n)\) is delayed by \(n_0\), \[y(n-n_0)=x\!\bigl[-(n-n_0)\bigr] \tag{vi}\] From equations (v) and (vi), \[y_1(n)\neq y(n-n_0)\] Thus, the system is time varying. (iv) From option (D): \(y(n)=x(n-3)\) Let input be delayed by \(n_0\). Then corresponding output is \[y_1(n)=x(n-n_0-3) \tag{vii}\] Now, output \(y(n)\) is delayed by \(n_0\), \[y(n-n_0)=x\!\bigl[(n-3)-n_0\bigr] \tag{viii}\] From equations (vii) and (viii), \[y_1(n)=y(n-n_0)\] Thus, the system is time invariant. (D) \(y[n]=x[n-3]\)

questions.question: The region of convergence of the Z-Transform of the discrete-time signal \(x[n]=2^{n}u[n]\) will be
questions.explanation:
Given \(x(n)=2^{n}u(n)\), a right-sided (causal) signal. \[X(z)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}x(n)z^{-n}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^{n}z^{-n}
=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\left(2z^{-1}\right)^{n}.\] This converges only if \(|2z^{-1}|<1\), i.e. \(|z|>2\), giving \[X(z)=\frac{1}{1-2z^{-1}}=\frac{z}{z-2},\qquad \text{ROC}:|z|>2.\] A) \(|z|>2\)

questions.question: Consider a discrete-time system for which the input \(x[n]\) and the output \(y[n]\) are related as, \[y[n]=x[n]-\frac{1}{3}y[n-1].\] If \(y[n]=0\) for \(n<0\) and \(x[n]=\delta[n]\), then \(y[n]\) can be expressed in terms of the unit step \(u[n]\) as
questions.explanation:
Given \(y(n)=x(n)-\dfrac{1}{3}y(n-1)\), \(x(n)=\delta(n)\), with \(y(n)=0\) for \(n<0\) (causal). Taking the Z-transform, \[Y(z)=1-\frac{1}{3}z^{-1}Y(z)
\ \Rightarrow\
Y(z)\left(1+\frac{1}{3z}\right)=1
\ \Rightarrow\
Y(z)=\frac{3z}{3z+1}=\frac{z}{z+\tfrac{1}{3}}.\] Taking the inverse Z-transform, \[y(n)=\left(-\frac{1}{3}\right)^{n}u(n).\] A) \(\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{n}u[n]\)

questions.question: In the circuit shown below, the ideality factor \(\eta\) of the diode is unity and the voltage drop across it is \(0.7\text{ V}\). The dynamic resistance of the diode at room temperature is approximately
questions.explanation: Since the diode is forward biased, it is ON with a constant voltage drop of \(V_D=0.7~\text{V}.\) Applying KVL, \[1.7-0.7-1~\text{k}\Omega\times I_D=0 \ \Rightarrow \ I_D = \frac{1}{1000} = 1~\text{mA}.\] The dynamic resistance of the diode is given by; \[r_d = \frac{\eta V_T}{I_D}.\] At room temperature, \[V_T\approx26~\text{mV}, \qquad \eta=1.\] Hence, \[r_d = \frac{1\times26~\text{mV}}{1~\text{mA}} = 26~\Omega \approx 25~\Omega.\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }25~\Omega}\]

questions.question: An ideal op-amp has the characteristics of an ideal
questions.explanation: An ideal operational amplifier produces an output voltage proportional to the difference between its two input voltages. \[V_{o}=A\left(V_{+}-V_{-}\right)\] where \(A\) is the open-loop voltage gain. Thus, the input quantity is a voltage and the output quantity is also a voltage. \[\boxed{\text{(a) Voltage Controlled Voltage Source}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the op-amp circuit shown below the input voltage \(V_{\text{in}}\) is gradually increased from \(-10\text{ V}\) to \(+10\text{ V}\). Assuming that the output voltage \(V_{\text{out}}\) saturates at \(-10\text{ V}\) and \(+10\text{ V}\), \(V_{\text{out}}\) will change from
questions.explanation: The circuit is an inverting Schmitt trigger. The non-inverting terminal receives positive feedback through the \(9\,\text{k}\Omega\)–\(1\,\text{k}\Omega\) divider. The reference voltage at the non-inverting terminal is \[V_{+}=\frac{1}{9+1}V_{o} =\frac{V_{o}}{10}\] Hence, the switching thresholds are \[V_{UT}=+\frac{10}{10}=+1\,\text{V}, \qquad V_{LT}=-\frac{10}{10}=-1\,\text{V}\] Initially, as \(V_{in}\) increases from \(-10\,\text{V}\), the output is at \[V_{o}=+10\,\text{V}\] Therefore, \[V_{+}=+1\,\text{V}\] The output changes state when \[V_{-}=V_{+}\] Since \(V_{-}=V_{in}\), \[V_{in}=+1\,\text{V}\] At this instant, the output switches from \[+10\,\text{V}\rightarrow-10\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{\text{(d) }+10\,\text{V}\text{ to }-10\,\text{V}\text{ when }V_{in}=+1\,\text{V}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: The op-amp circuit shown below is that of a
options: low-pass filter with a maximum gain of \(1\)
low-pass filter with a maximum gain of \(2\)
high-pass filter with a maximum gain of \(1\)
high-pass filter with a maximum gain of \(2\)
questions.explanation:
The circuit consists of a high-pass RC network followed by a non-inverting amplifier. The RC network connected to the non-inverting terminal has the transfer function \[\frac{V_{+}}{V_{in}} = \frac{sRC}{1+sRC}\] which is the standard first-order high-pass filter. The op-amp is configured as a non-inverting amplifier with \[R_f=1\,\text{k}\Omega,\qquad R_1=1\,\text{k}\Omega\] Hence, its voltage gain is \[A_v = 1+\frac{R_f}{R_1} = 1+\frac{1\,\text{k}\Omega}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} =2\] Therefore, the overall transfer function is \[\frac{V_o}{V_{in}} = 2\left(\frac{sRC}{1+sRC}\right)\] At low frequencies \((\omega\rightarrow0)\), \[\left|\frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\right|\rightarrow0\] and at high frequencies \((\omega\rightarrow\infty)\), \[\left|\frac{V_o}{V_{in}}\right|\rightarrow2\] Hence, the circuit is a high-pass filter with a maximum gain of 2. \[\boxed{\text{(d) High-pass filter with a maximum gain of }2}\]
Key points
  • A series capacitor followed by a resistor to ground forms a first-order high-pass filter.
  • Maximum passband gain is \(1+\dfrac{R_f}{R_1}\).

questions.question: A differential amplifier shown below has a differential mode gain of \(100\) and a CMRR of \(40\text{ dB}\). If \(V_1 = 0.55\text{ V}\) and \(V_2 = 0.45\text{ V}\), output is

For a practical differential amplifier, \[V_o=A_dV_d+A_cV_c\] where \[V_d=V_1-V_2=0.55-0.45=0.1\,\text{V}\] and the common-mode input is \[V_c=\frac{V_1+V_2}{2}
=\frac{0.55+0.45}{2}
=0.5\,\text{V}\] Given, \[A_d=100,\qquad
\text{CMRR}=40\,\text{dB}\] Using \[\text{CMRR}=20\log\left(\frac{A_d}{A_c}\right)\] \[40=20\log\left(\frac{100}{A_c}\right)\] \[\frac{100}{A_c}=10^2=100\] \[A_c=1\] Hence, \[V_o
=A_dV_d+A_cV_c
=(100)(0.1)+(1)(0.5)
=10+0.5
=10.5\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{\text{(b) }10.5\,\text{V}}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: In the amplifier circuit shown below, assume \(V_{BE}=0.7~\text{V}\) and the \(\beta\) of the transistor and the values of \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are extremely high. If the amplifier is designed such that at the quiescent point its \(V_{CE}=V_{CC}/2\), where \(V_{CC}\) is the power supply voltage, its small signal voltage gain \(\left|\dfrac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}\right|\) will be
questions.explanation:
Using the voltage divider, \[V_{th}=10\left(\frac{1.2}{8.8+1.2}\right)=1.2\,\text{V}\] Since \(V_{BE}=0.7\,\text{V}\), \[V_{E}=1.2-0.7=0.5\,\text{V}\] Given \(V_{CE}=V_{CC}/2=5\,\text{V}\), \[V_{C}=V_{E}+V_{CE}=0.5+5=5.5\,\text{V}\] Hence the voltage across \(R_{C}\) is \[10-5.5=4.5\,\text{V}\] Since \(\beta\) is very large, \[I_{C}\approx I_{E},\qquad R_{E}=\frac{0.5}{I_{E}},\qquad R_{C}=\frac{4.5}{I_{C}}\] Therefore, \[\frac{R_{C}}{R_{E}}=\frac{4.5}{0.5}=9\] Also, \[g_{m}R_{E}=\frac{I_{C}}{V_{T}}R_{E} =\frac{0.5}{25\,\text{mV}}\approx20\] The small-signal gain is \[A_{v}=\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} =-\frac{g_{m}R_{C}}{1+g_{m}R_{E}} =-\frac{20\times9}{21} \approx-8.57\] Hence, \[|A_{v}|\approx 9\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) }9}\]
Key points
  • The gain with an unbypassed emitter resistor is \(A_{v}=-\dfrac{g_{m}R_{C}}{1+g_{m}R_{E}}\)..

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: For a single stage BJT common base amplifier,
options: current gain as well as voltage gain can be greater than unity
current gain can be greater than unity but voltage gain is always less than unity
voltage gain can be greater than unity but current gain is always less than unity
current gain as well as voltage gain is always less than unity
questions.explanation: For a common-base (CB) amplifier, \[\text{Current gain }A_{i}=\alpha=\frac{I_{C}}{I_{E}}<1\] since \(\alpha\) is typically in the range \(0.98\) to \(0.998\). The voltage gain is \[A_{v}=g_{m}R_{C}\approx\frac{\alpha R_{C}}{r_{e}}\] As \(r_{e}\) is very small, \(A_{v}\) can be much greater than unity. Hence, in a CB amplifier, \[A_{i}<1,\qquad A_{v}>1\] \[\boxed{\text{(c) Voltage gain can be greater than unity but current gain is always less than unity}}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.ref: Representation of Boolean Expressions and K-Maps Q1
questions.question: The minimum SOP form of the Boolean expression \(y = \bar P \bar Q \bar R \bar S + P \bar Q \bar R \bar S +P \bar Q \bar R S +P \bar QRS +P \bar QR \bar S +\bar P \bar QR \bar S\) is:
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Given \(y = \bar P \bar Q \bar R \bar S + P \bar Q \bar R \bar S +P \bar Q \bar R S +P \bar QRS +P \bar QR \bar S +\bar P \bar QR \bar S\) \[y = \bar Q \bar R \bar S (P+\bar P ) + P \bar Q S (R+\bar R ) + \bar Q R \bar S (P+\bar P ) = \bar Q \bar R \bar S + P \bar Q S + \bar Q R \bar S\] \[y = \bar Q \bar S (\bar R +R) + P \bar Q S = \bar Q \bar S + P \bar Q S = \bar Q (\bar S + PS) = \bar Q (\bar S + P)\] \[y = \bar Q \bar S + P \bar Q\]
Method 2
Given \(y = \bar P \bar Q \bar R \bar S + P \bar Q \bar R \bar S +P \bar Q \bar R S +P \bar QRS +P \bar QR \bar S +\bar P \bar QR \bar S\). The expression can be written in minterm form as follows: \[y = \Sigma m (0,2,8,9,10,11)\] The K-Map is: Thus, minimized SOP expression is obtained as \(y = \bar Q \bar S + P \bar Q\)
\[\boxed{(A)\;\bar Q \bar S + P \bar Q }\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Make sure to check the 4 corners of the K-Map, since those terms may also form a quad.

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: The result of \((45)_{10}-(45)_{16}\) expressed in 2's complement representation is:
questions.explanation:
Given: \[N = (45)_{10} - (45)_{16} \quad \cdots (i)\] Converting \((45)_{16}\) to decimal: \[(45)_{16} = 4 \times 16^1 + 5 \times 16^0 = 64 + 5 = 69\] Substituting into equation \((i)\): \[N = (45)_{10} - (69)_{10} = (-24)_{10}\] Finding the 2's complement representation of \(-24\) in 6-bit form. First, represent \(+24\) in binary: \[+24 \rightarrow 011000\] Inverting all bits (1's complement): \[011000 \rightarrow 100111\] Adding 1 to get 2's complement: \[100111 + 1 = 101000\] \[\boxed{(C) \; 101000}\]
Key points
  • Alternatively, 2's complement can be found by keeping all trailing zeros and the rightmost 1 unchanged, then inverting all remaining bits to the left.
  • In 2's complement, the MSB is the sign bit: \(0\) for positive, \(1\) for negative.

questions.question: The output \(F\) of the multiplexer circuit shown below expressed int erms of the inputs \(P,Q\) and \(R\) is:
questions.explanation: From the given circuit , inputs are \[I_0 = R \;\; \;\;,  \;\;\;\;  I_1 =\bar R \;\; \;\;,  \;\;\;\;  I_2 =\bar R \;\; \;\;,  \;\;\;\;  I_3 = R\] Selection lines are \[S_1 = P\;\; \;\;,  \;\;\;\; S_0 = Q\] Thus final output equation is: \[F = \bar S_1 \bar S_0 I_0 + \bar S_1 S_0 I_1 + S_1 \bar S_0 I_2 + S_1 S_0 I_3\] \[F =  \bar P \bar QR +  \bar PQ \bar R + P \bar Q \bar R + PQR\] \[F = R \overline{(P \oplus Q)} + \bar R (P \oplus Q) = P \oplus Q \oplus R\] \[\boxed{(A) \; P \oplus Q \oplus R}\]

questions.question: If the multiplexer is controlled such that the channels are sequenced every 5 \(\mu\)s as 1 , 2 , 1 , 3 , 1 , 4 , 1 , 2 , 1 , 3 , 1 , 4 , 1 , ......, the input connected to channel 1 will be sampled at the rate of
questions.explanation: Given: Sequence of output \(Y\) is 1 , 2 , 1 , 3 , 1 , 4 , 1 , 2 , 1 , 3 , 1 , 4 , 1 , ..., and each output is generated after 5 \(\mu\)s. In the sequence, 1 is repeated every 10 \(\mu\)s. Therefore, \(T_s\) = 10 \(\mu\)s. Sampling frequency is given by: \[f_s = \frac{1}{T_s} = \frac{1}{10\; \mu \text{s}} = 100 \text{ k samples/s}\] \[\boxed{(C)\; \text{100k samples/s}}\]

questions.subject: digital-electronics
questions.question: A 2k x 8 bit RAM is interfaced to an 8-bit microprocessor. If the address of the first memory location in the RAM is 0800H, the address of the last memory location will be
questions.explanation:
Given: \(2\text{K} \times 8\)-bit memory interfaced to an 8-bit microprocessor; address of the first memory location \(= 0800\text{H}\).
Method 1
Total memory locations for a \(2\text{K} \times 8\) memory: \[2\text{K} \times 8\,\text{bits} = 2\text{K}\,\text{bytes} = 2 \times 1024 = 2048\,\text{bytes}\] Converting \(2048\) to hexadecimal: \[\begin{array}{r|ll} 16 & 2048 & \rightarrow 0 \\ \hline 16 & 128 & \rightarrow 0 \\ \hline 16 & 8 & \rightarrow 8 \\ \hline & 0 & \\ \end{array} \quad \implies \quad \text{Total memory locations} = 0800\text{H}\] Given the first location address \(= 0800\text{H}\). The final address is found using: \[\text{Total locations} = (\text{Final address} - \text{Initial address}) + 1\] \[\implies \text{Final address} = (\text{Total locations} + \text{Initial address}) - 1\] \[= (0800\text{H} + 0800\text{H}) - 1 = 1000\text{H} - 1 = 0\text{FFF}\text{H}\]
Method 2
For a \(2\text{K} \times 8\) (\(= 2^{11} \times 8\)) memory, \(11\) address lines (\(A_{10}\) to \(A_0\)) are required, giving a size of \(07\text{FF}\text{H}\). The last memory location is given by: \[\text{First memory location} + \text{Size of memory}(2\text{K} \times 8)\] \[0800\text{H} + 07\text{FF}\text{H} = 0\text{FFF}\text{H}\]
\[\boxed{(B)\; 0\text{FFF}\text{H}}\]
Key points
  • A memory of size \(N\text{k} \times 8\) requires \(\log_2(N \times 1024)\) address lines; the size in hex address span is \((N \times 1024 - 1)\), i.e., one less than the total location count due to zero-based addressing.
  • Standard sizes (in hex span): \(1\text{K} = 03\text{FF}\text{H}\), \(2\text{K} = 07\text{FF}\text{H}\), \(4\text{K} = 0\text{FFF}\text{H}\), \(8\text{K} = 1\text{FFF}\text{H}\) --- memorizing these accelerates address range problems.

questions.question:
Common data for Q3.08.1 and Q3.08.2 A unity feedback system has open loop transfer function \(G(s) = \dfrac{100}{s(s + p)}\). The time at which the response to a unit step input reaches its peak is \(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\) seconds.

The damping coefficient for the closed loop system is
questions.explanation: The closed-loop transfer function is expressed as: \[\frac{C(s)}{R(s)} = \frac{G(s)}{1 + G(s)} = \frac{100}{s^2 + ps + 100}\] Comparing this with the standard second-order characteristic equation \(s^2 + 2\xi\omega_n s + \omega_n^2 = 0\): \[\omega_n^2 = 100 \implies \omega_n = 10\,\text{rad/s}\] The peak time \(t_p\) for a unit step input is given by: \[t_p = \dfrac{\pi}{\omega_d} = \frac{\pi}{\omega_n\sqrt{1 - \xi^2}} = \frac{\pi}{8}\,\text{s}\] \[\frac{\pi}{10\sqrt{1 - \xi^2}} = \frac{\pi}{8}\] \[1 - \xi^2 = 0.64 \implies \xi = 0.6\] \[\boxed{(B) \ \ 0.6}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question:
Common data for Q3.08.1 and Q3.08.2 A unity feedback system has open loop transfer function \(G(s) = \dfrac{100}{s(s + p)}\). The time at which the response to a unit step input reaches its peak is \(\dfrac{\pi}{8}\) seconds.

The value of \(p\) is
questions.explanation: From the comparison of the characteristic equation in the previous question: \[s^2 + ps + 100 = s^2 + 2\xi\omega_n s + \omega_n^2 = 0\] Equating the coefficients of \(s\): \[p = 2\xi\omega_n\] Substituting the calculated values \(\omega_n = 10\,\text{rad/s}\) and \(\xi = 0.6\): \[p = 2 \times 0.6 \times 10 \implies p = 12\] \[\boxed{(B) \ \ 12}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: A closed loop control system is shown below. The range of the controller gain \(K_C\) which will make the real parts of all the closed loop poles more negative than \(-1\) is
questions.explanation:
The characteristic equation of the closed-loop system is: \(1 + G(s)H(s) = 0\) \[1 + \frac{K_c}{s(s+3)} = 0 \implies s^2 + 3s + K_c = 0\]
Method 1
The closed-loop poles are given by the roots: \[s_1, s_2 = \dfrac{-3 \pm \sqrt{9 - 4K_c}}{2}\] For the real parts of all poles to be more negative than \(-1\), we analyze the condition: \[\text{Re}(s_{1,2}) < -1\] Case 1: If the roots are complex conjugate (\(9 - 4K_c < 0\)), the real part is constant: \[\text{Re}(s_{1,2}) = -\frac{3}{2} = -1.5 < -1\] This holds true for any \(K_c > \dfrac{9}{4} = 2.25\). Case 2: If the roots are real (\(9 - 4K_c \ge 0\)), the dominant pole must satisfy: \[\frac{-3 + \sqrt{9 - 4K_c}}{2} < -1\] \[\sqrt{9 - 4K_c} < 1 \implies K_c > 2\] Combining with the condition \(K_c \le 2.25\) for real roots, we get \(2 < K_c \le 2.25\). Thus, for all cases, the condition \(K_c > 2\) must be satisfied.
Method 2
Alternatively, we can use the Routh-Hurwitz criterion by shifting the axis. To ensure all poles have real parts more negative than \(-1\), we substitute \(s = z - 1\): \[(z - 1)^2 + 3(z - 1) + K_c = 0\] \[z^2 + z + (K_c - 2) = 0\] Constructing the Routh-Hurwitz table for this \(z\)-domain polynomial:
\(z^2\)\(1\)\(K_c - 2\)
\(z^1\)\(1\)\(0\)
\(z^0\)\(K_c - 2\)
For the shifted system to be stable (all roots of \(z\) having negative real parts), there must be no sign changes in the first column of the Routh array. Therefore, all elements in the first column must be strictly positive: \[K_c - 2 > 0 \implies K_c > 2\]
\[\boxed{(C) \ \ K_C > 2}\]
Key points
To find the parameter range for poles located to the left of \(s = -\sigma\), shift the \(s\)-plane using the transformation \(s = z - \sigma\) and apply the Routh-Hurwitz criterion on the \(z\)-polynomial.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The open loop transfer function of a unity feedback system is \(G(s) = \dfrac{K(s + 2)}{(s + 1 + j1)(s + 1 - j1)}\). The root locus plot of the system has
options: two breakaway points located at \(s = -0.59\) and \(s = -3.41\)
questions.explanation: The open loop transfer function is given by: \[G(s)H(s) = \frac{K(s + 2)}{(s + 1 + j1)(s + 1 - j1)} = \frac{K(s + 2)}{s^2 + 2s + 2}\] For breakaway/break-in points, we set \(\dfrac{dK}{ds} = 0\): \[K = -\frac{s^2 + 2s + 2}{s + 2}\] Differentiating with respect to \(s\): \[\frac{dK}{ds} = -\frac{(2s + 2)(s + 2) - (s^2 + 2s + 2)(1)}{(s + 2)^2} = 0\] \[s^2 + 4s + 2 = 0\] Solving the quadratic equation: \[s = \frac{-4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 8}}{2} = -2 \pm \sqrt{2}; \ \ \ \ s_1 = -0.59 \quad \text{and} \quad s_2 = -3.41\] \(s = -3.41\) is a valid break-in point as it lies on the root locus. \[\boxed{\text{(C) one breakaway point located at $s = -3.41$}}\]

questions.question: For the closed loop system shown below to be stable, the value of time delay \(T_D\) (in seconds) should be less than
questions.explanation:
The open-loop transfer function is, \[G(s)=\frac{e^{-sT_D}}{s}\] \[G(j\omega)=\frac{1}{\omega}~\angle\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}-\omega T_D\right)\] The gain crossover frequency is obtained from, \[|G(j\omega_{gc})|=1\] \[\frac{1}{\omega_{gc}}=1\] \[\omega_{gc}=1~\text{rad/s}\] At the gain crossover frequency, \[\angle G(j1) =-\frac{\pi}{2}-T_D\] Hence, the phase margin is: \[PM =\pi+\angle G(j1) =\pi-\frac{\pi}{2}-T_D =\frac{\pi}{2}-T_D\] For the closed-loop system to be stable, \[PM>0\] \[\frac{\pi}{2}-T_D>0\] \[T_D<\frac{\pi}{2}\] \[\boxed{(C)\;\dfrac{\pi}{2}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not approximate the exponential term using Padé approximation when the problem can be solved directly using frequency-response concepts.
  • Do not mix degrees and radians while evaluating the phase contributed by the delay term.

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question: The Bode asymptotic plot of a transfer function is given below. In the frequency range shown, the transfer function has
questions.explanation: The slope of the Bode magnitude plot indicates the number of poles and zeros encountered at each corner frequency. Initially, the slope is \(0\,\text{dB/decade},\) which indicates that no pole or zero has been encountered. At \(\omega=\omega_1\), the slope changes from \(0\,\text{dB/decade}\) to \(+20\,\text{dB/decade}.\) An increase of \(20\,\text{dB/decade}\) corresponds to one zero. At \(\omega=\omega_2\), the slope changes from \(+20\,\text{dB/decade}\) to \(-20\,\text{dB/decade}.\) The change in slope is \(-20-(+20)=-40\,\text{dB/decade},\) which corresponds to two poles. Therefore, the transfer function contains \(1\) zero and \(2\) poles \[\boxed{(C)\;2\ \text{poles and}\ 1\ \text{zero}}\]

questions.subject: control-systems
questions.question:
The state space representation of a system is given by \[\dot{x}=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1\\
0 & -3
\end{bmatrix}x+
\begin{bmatrix}
1\\
0
\end{bmatrix}u\] \[y=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}x\] The transfer function \(\dfrac{Y(s)}{U(s)}\) of the system will be
questions.explanation:
Method 1
The transfer function of a state-space model is given by, \[G(s)=C(sI-A)^{-1}B+D\] Here, \[A= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad B= \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad C= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad D=0.\] Now, \[sI-A= \begin{bmatrix} s & -1\\ 0 & s+3 \end{bmatrix}\] \[(sI-A)^{-1} = \frac{1}{s(s+3)} \begin{bmatrix} s+3 & 1\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix}\] Therefore, \[C(sI-A)^{-1}B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \frac{1}{s(s+3)} \begin{bmatrix} s+3 & 1\\ 0 & s \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 0 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{s}\]
Method 2
The poles of the transfer function are the eigen values of the state matrix, \(A\) Here, \[A= \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 0 & -3 \end{bmatrix}\] \[|A|= \begin{vmatrix} 0 & 1\\ 0 & -3 \end{vmatrix} = 0\] Option (A): Pole is: \(s=0\) Option (B): Poles are: \(s=0,-3\) Option (C): Pole is: \(s=-3\) Option (D): Poles are: \(s=0,0\) Only option (A) matches. Therefore, the transfer function is \(\dfrac{1}{s}\)
\[\boxed{(A)\;\dfrac{1}{s}}\]
